changes.before: Write a low-specificity teal default for #notice that an ordinary later p rule can override to purple.
changes.after: Use :where() for a style that is easy to override.

before: :where() groups selector alternatives while contributing zero specificity, including its arguments. :is() can match the same elements but takes the specificity of its most specific argument. Here all rules are normal author rules in one layer.

The selector inside parentheses decides which elements match. :where(#notice) can match that ID without giving the rule ID-level specificity. The later p rule wins here. Replacing where with is gives the matching rule ID-level specificity, which outranks a type selector in this isolated comparison. Layers and importance are separate earlier cascade decisions.

Write a low-specificity teal default for #notice that an ordinary later p rule can override to purple. The supplied HTML stays in index.html; edit the CSS. The checks inspect this small page, not every possible browser or accessibility requirement. One supplied check inspects the authored :where(#notice) default as well as its computed result; another temporarily adds a later rule and then removes it.
after: Specificity is the selector strength CSS compares when earlier rule-order checks are tied. `:where()` matches the selectors inside it but adds zero specificity.
`:is()` can match the same elements. It gets the specificity of its strongest selector inside the parentheses. So `:is(#notice)` has ID-level strength, while `:where(#notice)` adds none.
Write the teal default with `:where(#notice)`. Keep the later purple rule. Replacing `where` with `is` would make the ID-based teal rule stronger in this example.
